text:
Photosynthesis converts light into chemical bonds stable enough to support the whole biosphere.

Antenna pigments pass the energy of absorbed light to P680, the reaction-center chlorophyll of photosystem II. P680 gives up an electron. Once oxidized, it pulls replacement electrons from water and releases O2 as a byproduct.

Electrons then travel through plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f, and photosystem I. This movement pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen, and the membrane holds them there. A pH gradient of roughly 3 units builds up and drives ATP synthase, which makes ATP.

ATP and NADPH are short-lived. They form within milliseconds and are used almost as fast. They power the Calvin cycle, where Rubisco fixes each CO2 at a cost of 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.

Glucose, the longer-term energy store, holds about 2,870 kJ/mol. Field measurements show that most sunlight never ends up there. Overall efficiency rarely exceeds 1–2%, because energy is lost at every step.
